column5: McKee on spectacle: technique (camera, effects, speed) carries meaning only when a story motivates it; 'abstractions are neutral' (editing rhythm applied to six scenes gives six meanings). Use as the course's warning that a technique must serve the story; quote no more than fifteen words.

McKee's unit ladder (beat, scene, sequence, act, story) gives coverage a test: each setup change is not a new scene unless the value at stake turns. Module 5 can teach: a cut between locations that leaves the value unchanged is a setup, not an event.

McKee's Archplot, Miniplot, Antiplot triangle: closed versus open endings, active versus passive protagonist, linear versus nonlinear time. Module 5 (editing and coverage) can use the time axis: a scrambled order of shots (Bad Timing) is a deliberate antistructure choice that must be named as such, not a default.

McKee: master the classical form before experimenting; the book's test is whether the writer can do the standard form on purpose. Suits the course's capstone order: shoot the conventional scene first, then break the rule with a stated reason.

McKee's setting dimensions (period, duration, location, level of conflict) map onto lighting and location choices: a period or location shot must match what that world would look like. Module 4 can add a research step: check the light, weather and interiors of the real setting before lighting it.

McKee's Fish Called Wanda example: two versions of one moment (paw only versus the gore) change whether the audience laughs. Module 5 can use it: the choice of insert or reaction shot sets the genre tone, so shoot the alternatives and test them on an audience.

McKee's genre conventions (the detective must apprehend, comedy nobody gets hurt) set audience expectation; lighting and colour follow the same contract. Module 4 can teach that a genre's look is a convention to honour, then vary, not a free choice of mood.

McKee: character is revealed by choices under pressure, not by characterization (looks, habits). For coverage, the camera's job is to hold the moment of choice: the reaction and the decision, not the setup. Module 5 can use this to decide which shot gets the time.

McKee: a story proves its idea by dramatising it, not explaining it. For editing, this is the case against captions and voice-over that state a meaning the images already carry; the cut between a positive and a negative beat is where the argument happens.

McKee's point that a didactic film fails by stacking the argument: for editing, a sequence built only to prove a point shows its hand. Balance the scenes that contradict the meaning as strongly as those that support it.

McKee separates sympathy (likeable) from empathy (the audience sees itself in the character). Coverage choice follows this: a subjective or close shot builds empathy, a distant shot builds judgement. Module 5 can give that choice a reason, not a habit.

McKee's Chinatown breakdown tracks shifts of point of view beat by beat (Gittes, then Evelyn, then Khan). For coverage, each shift of point of view is a shift of the camera's favour: a shot should sit with the character whose expectation has just been broken.

McKee's door example: a knock that is answered politely is dead screen time and the editor should cut to the next beat. Matches the course's pacing advice in module 5 on cutting out waiting; add the reason (no gap between expectation and result).

McKee's JAWS setup and payoff: the corpse on the beach must be found soon or the audience stops tracking the protagonist's imbalance (The River shows the cost of delay). Editing can use this: a setup shown early and paid off late reads as dead time unless the audience is kept aware of it.

McKee's rule for opening: the first major event within about the first quarter (a two-hour film, roughly the first half-hour), and exposition is shot then cut. Module 5 editing can say the same: shoot the opening exposition, expect to lose most of it, and cut to the event.

McKee's Ordinary People: the camera cuts from the mother's act to the father's face, so the reaction carries the Inciting Incident. Confirms the module 5 practice of holding the reaction shot after a disruptive act; the cut to the reaction is the event.

McKee's mid-film sag: a second act that repeats the first act's kind of action is treading water. Editing test for module 5: if two consecutive sequences would produce the same reaction, cut or merge one; a sag is usually a repeated beat, not a short one.

McKee's First Deadly Sin: alternating between two plots that never connect leaves the audience waiting for a link that never comes. Cross-cutting in module 5 needs a relation between the cut-away and the cut-to (causal or thematic), or it reads as confusion.

McKee's setup/payoff: a setup must carry one meaning when first seen and a deeper one when paid off (Cross saying 'my daughter'). Module 5 editing and coverage can plant this: a shot that is neutral on first view (a glance, a prop) gets a close-up later, so the insert pays off with meaning.

McKee's mood test: the same scene turns comic or thriller through light, colour, lens and casting (bright full shots versus night, tight canted shots, muted colour), with the events unchanged. Module 4 can cite this as the principle that light sets the mood while the scene's turn sets the emotion.

McKee's text/subtext split and the beat analysis (Casablanca's linen stall): a beat changes when behaviour changes, not when the dialogue does. Module 5 can use this to cut on the shift in behaviour, not on each line: hold the wide while the beat holds and cut in when the subtext turns.

McKee's beat-by-beat analysis can be used as a shot list: each beat's action/reaction pair names what the camera must hold (the action, then the reaction), and the Turning Point beat gets the longest hold. Module 5 coverage can teach this as a worked method.

McKee's rhythm: a location's visual interest is used up in roughly two or three minutes, after which the editor repeats the same establishing or two-shot. Module 5 can give this as a pacing rule of thumb (not a formula), with the rule that the big turn earns a longer hold, not a longer run of short scenes.

McKee's principle of transition: a link between two scenes is either held in common (a light, sound, action) or set in opposition (blue to red). This is the editor's match cut and contrast cut, given as a test: name the link before you cut.

McKee's Crisis is a deliberately static moment: the decision is held (Thelma and Louise stutter over go; Michael lowers the rifle) so tension builds before the action explodes. Module 5 can teach holding a shot on the decision and cutting on the action, not cutting faster into it. Slow motion and freeze are tools for this hold.

McKee's principle of antagonism: a protagonist is only as compelling as the forces against him, so build the opposition first. For the capstone, a film's visual opposition (the dark, the obstacle, the framing that blocks) is a design decision to plan, not an afterthought.

McKee on montage and voice-over: a montage is usually decorative editing that hides undramatised information, and the test for narration is to strip it out and see if the story still stands. For editing, the camera is an X-ray: a shot of a photograph montage tells the audience, it does not show it.

McKee's split between cheap and true surprise: a smash cut to a shock the story has not earned (the brother's nightmare in My Favorite Season) is a trick, while surprise that opens a gap and yields insight is story. Module 5 can give the test: a cut should reveal something the audience can understand afterwards, not just jolt.

McKee's four points of view for one scene (one character, the other, alternating, neutral profile) produce empathy for one, both, or laughter. Module 5 can make the camera's angle a deliberate choice: a neutral profile distances the audience and is the comic setup; a shot inside one character's view is the empathy setup.

McKee's test for a hole in logic: will the audience notice at the speed of the cut, or does it sit still on the page? For editing, continuity slips (a glance that breaks the line, a prop that moves) pass when the cut is fast; dwell on them and they break the film.

McKee on leaving room for the actor (subtext, not stage directions) and on one dominant contradiction: for the capstone, a shot should show the performer's choice, so frame and cut to let the subtext read, rather than to illustrate the line.

McKee's master-scene rule: write only the angles the story needs (an insert of the note only when the audience must read it with the character; otherwise stay on the master). Module 5 coverage can use it: shoot the master first, add inserts only for information the audience must see, and cut to a POV only when the view changes a choice.

McKee's image system: one category of image (water in Les Diaboliques, light and shadow in Casablanca) repeats with variation so it works below conscious notice. Module 4 can plan a colour or light motif per film (for example a recurring cool or warm source) and check it across the grade, not decorate each shot.
